evidence: The claim is supported by patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 3a-c.

claim: Local activation of interneurons in one cortical region during an up state causes a transition to the down state that occurs near synchronously in both recorded areas located ~2 mm apart.
source: Using simultaneous recordings of network and single cell activity in two brain regions located ~2 mm apart, we demonstrated that local activation of interneurons in one of the two regions during an up state causes a transition to the down state that occurs near synchronously in both recorded areas (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by simultaneous recording data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Photoactivation of interneurons in one cortical region promoted up-to-down transitions over large territories (up to 2 mm apart from the illuminated site) with latencies as short (~3 ms) as the ones characterizing spontaneous up-to-down transitions.

claim: The discharge of a small number (few tens) of APs in specific classes of local interneurons controls mesoscale state transitions in cortex.

evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The optogenetic manipulations interfered with ~40 APs in PV cells during down states.
source: From the data about spike activity of interneurons during down states reported in Figure 1, we then calculated that the optogenetic inhibitory manipulations displayed in Figure 4 interfered with ~40 APs in PV cells and about ~20 APs in SST interneurons during down states.
evidence: The claim is calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 4.

claim: The optogenetic manipulations interfered with about ~20 APs in SST interneurons during down states.
source: From the data about spike activity of interneurons during down states reported in Figure 1, we then calculated that the optogenetic inhibitory manipulations displayed in Figure 4 interfered with ~40 APs in PV cells and about ~20 APs in SST interneurons during down states.
evidence: The claim is calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 4.

claim: The GABAergic control of cortical state transition is surprisingly sensitive, with only a few tens of APs fired by interneurons efficiently controlling down-to-up state transition.
source: These results suggest that the GABAergic control of cortical state transition is surprisingly sensitive, with only a few tens of APs fired by interneurons efficiently controlling down-to-up state transition.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the calculation of the number of APs interfered with during optogenetic manipulations.

claim: The stronger effect of PV photo-inhibition on network activities might be related to the higher firing activity of PV cells compared to SST interneurons.

evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on experimental observations and citations to previous literature.

claim: The higher firing rate of SST cells in awake compared to anesthetized animals may explain the stronger effect of SST inhibition observed in awake compared to the anesthetized condition.
source: In line with this interpretation, the higher firing rate of SST cells in awake compared to anesthetized animals (Vyazovskiy et al., 2008) may also explain the stronger effect of SST inhibition observed in awake compared to the anesthetized condition (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on experimental observations and citation to previous literature (Vyazovskiy et al., 2008).

claim: Optogenetic inhibitory manipulation of SST interneurons triggered cortical state transitions that better resembled spontaneous transition compared to the same manipulation performed on PV cells.
source: Although the phase locking (Figure 2b,h) and phase speed analysis (Figure 2f,l) on simultaneous LFP and juxtasomal recordings do not show major differences between PV and SST cells, optogenetic inhibitory manipulation of SST interneurons triggered cortical state transitions that better resembled spontaneous transition compared to the same manipulation performed on PV cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of optogenetic manipulation effects shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: SST cells may have a more prominent role in regulating cortical state dynamics under physiological conditions.
source: These latter results could point to a more prominent role of SST cells in regulating cortical state dynamics under physiological conditions. This would be in line with recent findings demonstrating that SST firing activity is extremely sensitive to cortical states and strongly affected by cholinergic inputs from subcortical areas (Gentet et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2015; Muñoz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on experimental observations and citations to recent literature (Gentet et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2015; Muñoz et al., 2017).

claim: Early activation of thalamic nuclei may contribute to the generation of up states by early activation of fast spiking (FS) cells followed stimulation of pyramidal neurons.
source: In this regard, it is interesting to note that spiking activity of thalamic nuclei have been reported to occur during cortical down states ahead of up state initiation and it has been proposed that the early activation of thalamic nuclei contributes to the generation of up states by early activation of fast spiking (FS) cells followed stimulation of pyramidal neurons (Ushimaru and Kawaguchi, 2015).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis from previous literature (Ushimaru and Kawaguchi, 2015).

claim: Early activation of FS interneurons may actually prevent, rather than favour, the up state initiation.
source: Our data are compatible with these experimental findings, but suggest that early activation of FS interneurons may actually prevent, rather than favour, the up state initiation.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Weak thalamic activation during cortical down states preferentially induces suprathreshold activity in cortical FS interneurons leading to a prolongation of the silent cortical state.
source: While it is clear that strong thalamic activation by means of electrical (MacLean et al., 2005; Reig and Sanchez-Vives, 2007; Reig et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2008) or sensory (Petersen et al., 2003a; Hasenstaub et al., 2007; Civillico and Contreras, 2012) stimulation is a trigger for down-to-up state transitions in cortex, our data are compatible with the scenario in which weak thalamic activation during cortical down states preferentially induces suprathreshold activity in cortical FS interneurons (Hu and Agmon, 2016) leading to a prolongation of the silent cortical state.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the experimental data and citations to previous literature (MacLean et al., 2005; Reig and Sanchez-Vives, 2007; Reig et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2008; Petersen et al., 2003a; Hasenstaub et al., 2007; Civillico and Contreras, 2012; Hu and Agmon, 2016).

claim: SST interneurons may be similarly controlled by thalamic inputs.
source: In this framework, the observation that SST interneurons are also active during cortical down states suggests that these interneuronal cells may be similarly controlled by thalamic inputs (Tan et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on experimental observations and citation to previous literature (Tan et al., 2008).

claim: A sudden withdrawal of activity in a confined cortical area can trigger synchronous mesoscale network transitions towards silent states.

evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on local optogenetic manipulation.

claim: Local inhibition plays a role in the control of down state synchrony across cortical areas.
source: Moreover, our data also show that photo-inhibition of interneurons during an ongoing up state significantly affects network activity at distal cortical locations. When interneurons were locally inhibited in one region during a down state a transition to the up state was reliably observed in two recorded areas located >2 mm apart (Figure 6e,f,k,l), directly demonstrating a role of local inhibition in the control of down state synchrony across cortical areas.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 6e,f,k,l.

claim: Activity of PV interneurons causally contributes to terminate cortical up states.
source: In the present study we demonstrate that activity of the two major subtypes of cortical interneurons, the PV and the SST positive cells, causally contribute to terminate cortical up states.
evidence: The claim is a main conclusion of the study supported by multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Activity of SST interneurons causally contributes to terminate cortical up states.

claim: Interneurons control the down-to-up transition.

evidence: The claim is a main conclusion of the study supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: The weak firing activity of interneurons during cortical down state is fundamental to maintain the cortical circuitry in the silent state, preventing it from escaping into the up state.

evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the experimental data showing interneuron firing during down states and the effects of their inhibition.
